Gkeyll has a Jenkins-based CI system implemented in ci/jenkins/. At the moment if a user wants to acknowledge deliberate changes in a regression test (say because they deliberately changed the algorithm and the results are expected to change relative to main) they have to list such test in expected_regression_diffs.txt.

One issue we are running into is that a PR (say PR #1) may list some tests in this file. Then this PR gets merged into main and this version of expected_regression_diffs.txt, with some tests listed, is now in main. But then a later PR (say PR #2) is opened by another person completely unaware of the work in PR #1, and that person has to remember to delete the tests that PR #1 placed in expected_regression_diffs.txt. If they don't remember to delete them, PR #2 doesn't run tests that it should've run.

Can you come up with a better system, so that the list of tests expected to produce different results in one PR doesn't get dragged into future PRs, posibly causing some tests to not be run?

I’ll inspect the Jenkins CI flow and the existing allow-list semantics first, then pin down a design that is safe across merges and PR rebuilds. I’ll use the repository’s CI layout rather than assume how GitHub/Jenkins metadata is currently exposed.

Thus entries already merged into `main` are automatically inert for every later PR (and for `main` itself), without requiring anyone to remove them. Yes. A cleanup-only PR can delete stale lines; because deletions never form an active acknowledgment, the cleanup has no waiver effect but leaves `main` tidy after merge.

For the corner case where a PR deliberately changes a test that already has a stale entry on `main`, I’d treat an edited/replaced acknowledgment line (including its reason) as a newly requested waiver. That lets the author both refresh the rationale and explicitly acknowledge the new change, while an untouched inherited line stays inert.

<proposed_plan>
# PR-scoped regression acknowledgments

## Summary

Make acknowledgments effective only when they are new or updated relative to the exact baseline checkout. All regression tests still run; this only controls whether a reported difference fails CI.

## Key changes

- Extend `check_regression_results.lua` with an optional baseline acknowledgment-file argument, preserving the current three-argument interface for standalone callers.
- Parse candidate and baseline entries as normalized full non-comment lines. A candidate entry waives a test only when that full line is absent from the baseline file.
  - Unchanged entries inherited from `main` are inert.
  - Deleting old entries is a safe cleanup-only change.
  - Replacing a line with an updated reason is a fresh, active acknowledgment, as agreed.
- Run the checker from the baseline/trusted checkout against the candidate results and candidate acknowledgment file. This avoids dependence on an older PR branch’s checker implementation during rollout.
- Update the personal Jenkins flow and both Stellar/Perlmutter serial and parallel Slurm payloads to pass the baseline file at `_baseline/ci/jenkins/expected_regression_diffs.txt`.
- Update CI documentation and report wording to state that only candidate-new or candidate-updated entries are honored; stale lines may be removed in any later PR.

## Test plan

- Add a lightweight checker test using a temporary SQLite regression database to verify:
  - a newly added candidate entry acknowledges a failing test;
  - an unchanged inherited entry does not;
  - deleting an inherited entry has no acknowledgment effect;
  - changing an inherited line’s reason creates a fresh acknowledgment.
- Validate each Jenkins backend’s serial and parallel invocation supplies the baseline file.
- Validate the CI change in the documented trusted-CI staging job before merging.

## Assumptions

- `expected_regression_diffs.txt` remains a reviewable repository file; it may contain historical entries temporarily, but inherited entries cannot mask failures.
- A refreshed reason is an intentional, reviewable request to acknowledge a new difference for that test.
</proposed_plan>

<proposed_plan>
# Fail-fast stale-baseline guard for Jenkins CI

## Summary

Before any dependency, compilation, or regression work, verify that the exact resolved baseline commit is an ancestor of the exact candidate commit. Fail stale comparisons immediately by default; allow an explicit, auditable override for intentional historical comparisons. Apply this to personal, Stellar, Perlmutter, and team-workstation CI.

## Implementation changes

- Add `ALLOW_STALE_BASELINE` (default `false`) to the personal, Stellar, and Perlmutter Jenkins parameters. The shared personal pipeline will enforce it for team-workstation CI too.
- Add `--allow-stale-baseline` to all CI launch clients and the unified CLI help; forward it as the Jenkins boolean parameter. Show the setting in queued/recent build summaries.
- After the cheap candidate checkout and before any build stage:
  - resolve and pin the baseline to a full commit SHA;
  - compare the resolved baseline and candidate SHAs through GitHub’s compare API;
  - continue only when the candidate contains the baseline, or when `ALLOW_STALE_BASELINE=true`.
- For PRs, use the PR API’s base commit SHA; for manual branch selectors, resolve the branch to a SHA before comparison. Build the pinned SHA later, preventing branch movement during a long run from changing what CI tests.
- On a blocked comparison, terminate before dependency setup, write a preflight artifact with both SHAs and the reason, and publish a concise status/report explaining that the candidate must merge or rebase the baseline. On override, record the bypass in the same artifact and report.
- Fail closed if ancestry cannot be established; users can use the explicit override for an intentional run during a GitHub API outage.

## Test plan

- Validate a candidate containing the baseline proceeds and records pinned candidate/baseline SHAs.
- Validate a stale PR and a stale manual ref comparison fail before any build or Slurm submission.
- Validate `--allow-stale-baseline` permits the same stale comparison and records the bypass.
- Validate a baseline advancing after preflight does not alter the pinned baseline checkout.
- Stage the trusted Jenkinsfile changes on each platform before merge.

## Assumptions

- “Up to date” means the resolved baseline commit is an ancestor of the resolved candidate commit.
- The override is available for any PR or manual candidate/baseline comparison, but is never enabled automatically.
</proposed_plan>

Before any dependency, compilation, or regression work, verify that the exact resolved baseline commit is an ancestor of the exact candidate commit. Require `GKEYLL_CI_ROOT` in Jenkins global environment for every CI flavor. Cache one complete baseline per platform under:

- `$GKEYLL_CI_ROOT/baseline-cache/<platform>/current`
- `$GKEYLL_CI_ROOT/last-candidate-results/<platform>`

They are separate today because serial and MPI-parallel regressions need materially different Slurm allocations.

- Stellar serial regression uses one task with 8 CPUs. Its MPI lane uses 4 tasks with 1 CPU each.
- Perlmutter serial regression uses 1 GPU and 32 CPUs. Its MPI lane uses 4 tasks, each with 1 GPU and 8 CPUs—four GPUs total.

Combining them into one allocation would reserve the larger parallel allocation for the whole job. On Perlmutter, three GPUs would sit idle while serial tests run; on Stellar, many allocated CPUs would be idle. It can also queue longer, needs a combined walltime limit, and makes a serial failure prevent the parallel lane from running.

The advantage of combining is only one scheduler submission and potentially one queue wait. Separate jobs let each lane request precisely what it needs, isolate failures, and preserve the existing two-job candidate path. For that reason, I recommend keeping serial and parallel lanes separate; a cache miss adds one baseline-generation job per lane, while a cache hit remains the current two candidate jobs.

content.text:
The split is not because candidate checking technically needs a separate allocation. It is to make cache publication independent of the candidate outcome.

Today, each lane does:

```text
create baseline output → check candidate output → fail the Slurm job if candidate differs
```

If kept combined, a deliberate or accidental candidate regression makes the job fail after creating baseline data. Jenkins then stops before the other lane may run, and cannot safely publish a complete serial-plus-parallel baseline cache. That is exactly the common case where retaining the generated baseline would be most useful for a follow-up candidate commit.

With separate jobs, the dependency is:

```text
generate serial baseline ─┐
                          ├─ publish complete baseline cache ─┬─ candidate serial check
generate parallel baseline┘                                   └─ candidate MPI check
```

Thus baseline creation can succeed and be retained even if either candidate check fails or is aborted. The cache is also never exposed to candidate-side commands that could alter it.

It is possible to retain two combined jobs, but that requires both scripts and Jenkins to capture candidate failures without failing immediately, force the other lane to run, verify both baseline products, publish the cache, and only then report the stored candidate failure. That is more fragile failure handling for a CI path whose primary job is accurate failure reporting.

Keeping baseline generation separate makes cache publication independent of candidate failures. It ensures both serial and parallel baseline results are complete and verified before candidate checks run.
